verses.text: After this, Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, with fifty men to run ahead of him.

He got up early and stood by the road to the city gate. Whenever someone came to have the king rule on a dispute, Absalom called out, “What town are you from?” The person would say which tribe of Israel he belonged to.
Absalom would tell him, “You've got a valid case, but the king hasn't appointed anyone to hear you.”
Then he'd say, “If only I were made judge in this land! Anyone with a dispute could come to me, and I'd see that they got justice.”
Whenever someone came up to bow to him, Absalom would reach out, take hold of him, and kiss him.
Absalom treated all the Israelites who came to the king for a ruling this way. That's how he stole the hearts of the people of Israel.
At the end of forty years, Absalom said to the king, “Please let me go to Hebron to fulfill a vow I made to the LORD.
While I was staying in Geshur in Syria, I vowed, ‘If the LORD really brings me back to Jerusalem, I'll serve him.’”
“Go in peace,” the king told him. So Absalom left for Hebron.
But Absalom sent spies through all the tribes of Israel with this message: “As soon as you hear the trumpet, say, ‘Absalom is king in Hebron!’”
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom as invited guests. They went in good faith and knew nothing about the plot.
While Absalom was offering sacrifices, he sent to Giloh for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's adviser. The conspiracy gained strength as more and more people joined Absalom.
A messenger came to David and said, “The people of Israel have given their hearts to Absalom.”

David told all his servants with him in Jerusalem, “Get up! We have to run, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Hurry, before he catches us, brings disaster on us, and attacks the city with the sword.”
The king's servants answered, “We're ready to do whatever my lord the king decides.”
The king left with his whole household following him. He left ten of his concubines behind to look after the palace.
The king went out with all the people following, and they stopped at Beth Merhak.
All his servants filed past him, including all the Cherethites and Pelethites. The six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath also marched past the king.
The king asked Ittai from Gath, “Why are you coming with us too? Go back and stay with the king. You're a foreigner and an exile. Go back to where you've been living.
You only came yesterday. Should I make you wander with us today when I don't even know where I'm going? Go back and take your people with you. May mercy and faithfulness be with you.”
Ittai answered the king, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as my lord the king lives, wherever you are, your servant will be there too, whether it means life or death.”
David told Ittai, “Go ahead and cross.” So Ittai from Gath crossed over with all his men and the children who were with him.
Everyone in the countryside wept aloud as the people passed. The king himself crossed the Kidron Valley stream, and all the people went across toward the wilderness.
Zadok came too, with all the Levites carrying the ark of God's covenant. They set God's ark down, and Abiathar went up while the last of the people made their way out of the city.
The king told Zadok, “Take God's ark back to the city. If the LORD looks on me with favor, he'll bring me back and let me see it again and the place where he dwells.
But if he says, ‘I take no delight in you,’ here I am. Let him do whatever he sees fit with me.”
The king also told Zadok the priest, “Aren't you a seer? Go back into the city in peace with the two young men, your son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan.
I'll wait at the wilderness crossings until you send me word.”
So Zadok and Abiathar took God's ark back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
David climbed the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare. Everyone with him covered their heads and wept as they went up.
Someone told David, “Ahithophel is part of Absalom's plot.” David prayed, “LORD, please turn Ahithophel's advice into foolishness.”
When David reached the summit, where people worshiped God, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his tunic torn and dirt on his head.
David told him, “If you come with me, you'll be a burden.
But if you go back to the city and tell Absalom, ‘I'll serve you, Your Majesty. Just as I served your father before, I'll serve you now,’ you can undermine Ahithophel's advice for me.
You'll have the priests Zadok and Abiathar there. Tell them everything you hear from the palace.
Their two sons are there with them, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send me everything you hear through them.”
So Hushai, David's friend, entered the city as Absalom arrived in Jerusalem.
